q: Cathode rays are fast moving ____ emitted from the cathode of a discharge tube.
e: Cathode rays are streams of fast-moving electrons observed in vacuum tubes.

q: They were discovered while studying the electric discharge through gases at ____ pressure.
e: Electric discharge through gases is studied at low pressure to observe cathode rays.

q: Electric discharge first occurs at about ____ Hg.
e: The initial electric discharge in the tube occurs at a pressure of about 20 mm Hg.

q: As the pressure is reduced further, at very low pressure(~0.01 mm Hg) glass behind the positive electrode(____) is observed to glow.
e: The glow appears behind the positive electrode, which is the anode, due to rays striking the glass.

q: Cathode rays were first observed in 1869 by Julius Plucker and Johann Hittorf, and were named in 1876 by ____ as cathode rays.
e: Eugen Goldstein named these rays 'cathode rays' in 1876.

q: In 1897, British physicist ____ showed that cathode rays composed of a previously unknown negatively charged particle, which was later named the electron.
e: J.J. Thomson discovered the electron by studying the properties of cathode rays.

q: He measured the charge to mass ratio (e/m) of electron and found to be ____.
e: Thomson's measurement of the charge-to-mass ratio was a key step in identifying the electron.

q: Combining with the charge of the electron $-1.602\times 10^{-19}\text{C}$ (measured by ____ in 1906), the mass of the electron is $9.107\times 10^{-31}\text{kg}$.
e: Millikan's oil drop experiment accurately measured the charge of the electron.

q: From the experiment with cathode rays it is found that cathode rays travel in ____ lines.
e: Cathode rays travel in straight lines, as evidenced by sharp shadows formed by obstacles in their path.

q: From the experiment with cathode rays it is found that cathode rays have ____ and kinetic energy.
e: Cathode rays can turn a paddle wheel, demonstrating they possess momentum and kinetic energy.

q: From the experiment with cathode rays it is found that cathode rays can be deflected by both electric and ____ fields.
e: Because they are charged particles, cathode rays are deflected by both electric and magnetic fields.

q: From the experiment with cathode rays it is found that cathode rays can ____ the gases through which they pass.
e: Cathode rays have enough energy to strip electrons from gas atoms, causing ionization.

q: From the experiment with cathode rays it is found that cathode rays can produce ____.
e: When cathode rays strike certain materials, they cause them to glow, a phenomenon called fluorescence.

q: The cathode ray tube(CRT) is a vacuum tube that contains an electron gun, a deflection system and a ____ screen, and is used to display images.
e: The fluorescent screen in a CRT glows when struck by the focused electron beam.

q: Before late 2000 AD, CRTs are widely used in cathode ray oscilloscopes (____), television sets and computer monitors.
e: CROs (Cathode Ray Oscilloscopes) were a primary application of CRT technology.

q: Since then CRTs have been largely superseded by newer flat-panel display technologies such as liquid crystal display(LCD), plasma display, and organic light-emitting diode (____) displays.
e: OLED is one of the modern flat-panel display technologies that replaced bulky CRTs.

q: Cathode rays are ____.
e: Cathode rays themselves cannot be seen; only their effects, like fluorescence, are visible.

q: However, when cathode rays struck the glass wall of a tube or a fluorescent screen they can cause a glow called ____.
e: The visible glow produced when cathode rays hit a fluorescent material is called fluorescence.

q: X-rays are electromagnetic waves like light, but their wavelengths are much ____ than those of light.
e: X-rays have much shorter wavelengths and higher frequencies than visible light.

q: Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen discovered X-rays in ____ while experimenting with cathode rays.
e: Wilhelm Conrad Roentgen made the accidental discovery of X-rays in 1895.

q: Because he did not know what the rays were, he called them X-rays, meaning ____ rays.
e: The 'X' in X-rays stands for unknown, as their nature was initially a mystery.

q: Later experiments revealed that X-rays are electromagnetic waves which have a wavelength in the range of ____ to 10 nanometre (nm).
e: The wavelength of X-rays typically ranges from 0.01 nm to 10 nm.

q: They are shorter in wavelength than ultraviolet (UV) rays and longer than ____ rays.
e: In the electromagnetic spectrum, X-rays lie between UV rays and gamma rays.

q: X-rays of energy about 0.1 to 10 keV (wavelength 10 to 0.10 nm) are classified as ____ X-rays.
e: Soft X-rays have lower energy and lower penetrating power.

q: X-rays of energy about 10 to 100keV(wavelength 0.10 to 0.01nm) are classified as ____ X-rays, due to their penetrating abilities.
e: Hard X-rays have higher energy and greater penetrating power.

q: 1 electron volt (eV) = ____ J is an energy unit used in atomic and nuclear physics.
e: One electron volt is the energy gained by an electron accelerating through a potential difference of one volt.

q: An X-ray tube consists of a cathode and a target (____).
e: The target in an X-ray tube acts as the anode, where electrons strike to produce X-rays.

q: A high potential difference (about 10-100 kV) is applied between target and cathode to ____ electrons emitted from the cathode.
e: The high voltage accelerates electrons to high speeds before they hit the target.

q: X-rays are produced when high-energy electrons strike the target which is made of a high dense material such as ____.
e: Tungsten is commonly used as the target material due to its high density and high melting point.

q: X-rays have no charge, cannot be deflected by both electric and ____ fields.
e: As electromagnetic waves, X-rays are neutral and are not deflected by electric or magnetic fields.

q: They travel through vacuum with the speed of ____.
e: Like all electromagnetic waves, X-rays travel at the speed of light in a vacuum.

q: They have high ____ power.
e: X-rays can pass through many materials that are opaque to visible light.

q: Hence, thick dense shielding, such as high density concrete or ____ is necessary to protect against X-rays.
e: Lead is highly effective at absorbing X-rays and is used for radiation shielding.

q: Soft tissue(like organs and skin) cannot absorb the X-rays; however high density materials(such as ____) absorb X-rays.
e: Bones absorb X-rays, creating the contrast seen in medical X-ray photographs.

q: X-rays can cause ____ by stripping electrons from the atoms and can cause biological effects.
e: X-rays are ionizing radiation, which can damage living tissue.

q: X-rays consist of high energy ____ which are energy packets of electromagnetic wave.
e: X-rays exhibit particle-like behavior, consisting of high-energy photons.

q: soft X-rays (low penetrating power) are used to take X-ray photographs of some parts of ____.
e: Soft X-rays are ideal for medical imaging of the human body.

q: Hard X-rays (high penetrating power) are used to destroy ____ cells.
e: The high energy of hard X-rays is utilized in radiation therapy to target and destroy cancer cells.

q: X-rays are used in industries for finding defects in welded joints and metal ____.
e: Industrial radiography uses X-rays to inspect metal castings for internal flaws.

q: Since X-rays can exhibit wave nature, they are used to determine the structure of ____.
e: X-ray diffraction is a key technique for analyzing crystal structures.

q: X-rays are also used in security systems to reveal hidden unlawful materials (such as weapons and ____).
e: Airport and border security scanners use X-rays to detect concealed contraband.

q: X-rays can be classified as two types: (i) characteristic X-rays (intense sharp lines) and (ii) continuous X-rays (or) ____ X-rays.
e: Continuous X-rays are also referred to as white X-rays because they contain a continuous spectrum of wavelengths.

q: When a high energy electron emitted from the cathode bombard the target material, it may knock an electron in the ____-shell of an atom completely out of its orbit.
e: Characteristic X-rays are produced when an inner-shell electron is ejected.

q: When outer-shell electrons, having higher energy, fill the vacancy in the inner shell, the energy is released in the form of ____.
e: The energy difference between the outer and inner shells is emitted as a characteristic X-ray photon.

q: These X-rays are called characteristic X-rays because they have specific energies characteristic of the element used as the ____.
e: The energy of characteristic X-rays depends on the atomic structure of the target material.

q: When an electron striking the target passes through the atoms of the target material, it will suffer a retarding force in the ____ field of the nuclei of the target.
e: The Coulomb field of the nucleus causes the incoming electron to decelerate.

q: When this occurs, the electron will lose some of its ____ energy and the energy is released in the form of X-rays.
e: The loss of kinetic energy during deceleration is converted into continuous X-ray photons.

q: Continuous X-rays are also called ____ radiation (braking radiation) according to the phenomenon they are produced.
e: Bremsstrahlung is the German word for 'braking radiation', describing the deceleration of electrons.

q: Rutherford's model states that an atom has a central ____ and an electron or electrons revolve around it.
e: Rutherford proposed the nuclear model of the atom with a dense central nucleus.

q: However, according to electromagnetic theory, accelerating charged particles, i.e., the orbiting electrons will emit radiation and finally they will collapse into the ____.
e: Classical physics predicted that orbiting electrons would lose energy and spiral into the nucleus.

q: In order to overcome this drawback of Rutherford's atomic model, ____ proposed a new model.
e: Niels Bohr introduced quantum concepts to resolve the stability issue of Rutherford's model.

q: Bohr postulated that in an atom, an electron can move only in allowed ____ orbits.
e: Bohr's first postulate restricts electrons to specific, stable circular orbits.

q: If an electron is moving in such an orbit, it does not absorb(or) emit ____.
e: Electrons in stationary orbits do not radiate energy, ensuring atomic stability.

q: The atom can exist in certain stable states with a definite total ____.
e: These stable states are called stationary states, each with a specific energy level.

q: An electron revolves around the nucleus in circular orbits with angular momentum L which is an integral multiple of ____.
e: Bohr's second postulate quantizes the angular momentum of the electron.

q: This postulate is the concept of angular momentum ____.
e: Quantization means the angular momentum can only take discrete, specific values.

q: An electron can undergo transition from an orbit to another by absorbing (or) emitting energy which is equal to the energy ____ between the two states.
e: Bohr's third postulate states that energy is absorbed or emitted during transitions between orbits.

q: An electron of charge e and mass m moving in a circular orbit of radius r experiences the centripetal force balanced by the attractive ____ force between electron and proton (nucleus).
e: The electrostatic Coulomb force provides the necessary centripetal force for the electron's orbit.

q: According to the Bohr's postulate II, L=mvr=____.
e: This is the mathematical expression for the quantization of angular momentum, where n is an integer.

q: The total energy of hydrogen atom is E=kinetic energy KE + ____ energy PE.
e: The total energy is the sum of the electron's kinetic and potential energies.

q: According to Eq.(12.4), all the energy values are ____ which means electron is bound to the nucleus.
e: Negative energy indicates that work must be done to remove the electron from the atom.

q: Here we would introduce an important constant, which is fine structure constant ____ (a dimensionless constant).
e: The fine structure constant is a fundamental physical constant characterizing the strength of electromagnetic interactions.

q: The ground state energy of hydrogen atom is ____ eV.
e: The lowest energy level (n=1) of the hydrogen atom is -13.6 eV.

q: Energy of hydrogen atom in the nth state E = ____ eV (n=1, 2, 3, ...).
e: This formula gives the quantized energy levels of the hydrogen atom.

q: Radius of hydrogen atom r = ____ $n^2$ Å.
e: The radius of the electron's orbit increases with the square of the principal quantum number n.

q: For n=1, the radius of hydrogen atom is called Bohr's ____(rB), r = 0.52896 Å.
e: The Bohr radius is the most probable distance between the nucleus and the electron in a hydrogen atom's ground state.

q: A hydrogen discharge tube is a slim tube containing hydrogen gas at ____ pressure with an electrode at each end.
e: Low pressure is required for the gas to discharge and emit light when high voltage is applied.

q: If a high voltage is applied, the tube lights up with a bright ____ glow.
e: Excited hydrogen gas emits a characteristic bright pink glow.

q: Bohr's model explains the spectral lines of the hydrogen atomic ____ spectrum.
e: Bohr's model successfully predicted the wavelengths of the hydrogen emission spectrum.

q: When the atom gains energy, the electron jumps from the ground state to another state with ____ energy.
e: Absorption of energy excites the electron to a higher energy level.

q: Energy levels are designated with an integer n which is called principal ____ number.
e: The principal quantum number n determines the energy and size of the electron's orbit.

q: The ground state is ____, the first excited state is n=2, and so on.
e: The lowest possible energy state of the atom is the ground state, where n=1.

q: The energy gained by the atom is equal to the ____ in energy between the two energy levels.
e: The energy of the absorbed or emitted photon exactly matches the energy gap between orbits.

q: When the electron returns back from the higher energy state to a lower energy state, it releases energy that is equal to the difference in energy of the two ____.
e: This released energy corresponds to the difference between the initial and final orbital energy levels.

q: The energy ΔE is released in the form of an electromagnetic radiation with ____.
e: The frequency of the emitted radiation is directly proportional to the energy difference (ΔE = hv).

q: Radiated energy ΔE = hv = hc/λ = ____ - En_f, and n_i > n_f.
e: The energy of the emitted photon is the difference between the initial energy state ($E_{n_i}$) and the final energy state ($E_{n_f}$).

q: As the energy increases further and further from the nucleus, the spacing between the levels gets ____ and ____.
e: Energy levels become more closely spaced as the principal quantum number n increases.

q: In the emission of X-rays, the energy emitted due to electron transition from n=2 energy state to n=1 energy state is ____ characteristic X-rays.
e: A transition from the L shell (n=2) to the K shell (n=1) produces $K_\alpha$ X-rays.

q: whereas a transition from n=3 energy state to n=1 energy state is ____ characteristic X-rays.
e: A transition from the M shell (n=3) to the K shell (n=1) produces higher energy $K_\beta$ X-rays.

q: When electromagnetic radiation(e.g.light) of sufficient energy incident on the metal surface the ____ are ejected from its surface.
e: The photoelectric effect involves the ejection of electrons from a metal surface by light.

q: This phenomenon is known as ____ effect.
e: The emission of electrons due to incident electromagnetic radiation is called the photoelectric effect.

q: These ejected electrons are called ____.
e: Electrons emitted as a result of the photoelectric effect are specifically termed photoelectrons.

q: There are no electrons emitted below a certain frequency of incident light which is different for different ____.
e: The threshold frequency depends on the specific work function of the metal.

q: This frequency is called the ____ frequency $v_0$.
e: The minimum frequency required to eject electrons from a metal surface is the threshold frequency.

q: Photoelectric current is directly proportional to ____ of the incident light.
e: Higher light intensity means more photons, which ejects more electrons, increasing the current.

q: The kinetic energy of photoelectrons is directly proportional to ____ of the incident light.
e: According to Einstein's photoelectric equation, maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency of the incident light.

q: The photoelectric effect cannot be explained by considering light as a ____.
e: Classical wave theory fails to explain the threshold frequency and instantaneous emission of photoelectrons.

q: However, this phenomenon can be explained by the ____ nature of light, in which light can be visualized as a stream of particles of electromagnetic energy.
e: Einstein explained the photoelectric effect by proposing that light consists of discrete particles called photons.

q: These particles are called ____.
e: Photons are the fundamental quanta of light.

q: The energy of a photon is related to the frequency of light as, E=____.
e: Planck's equation states that the energy of a photon is directly proportional to its frequency.

q: where E is the energy of the photon, h is ____ constant, v is the frequency of light, c is the speed of light (in a vacuum) and λ is the wavelength of the light.
e: Planck's constant is the proportionality factor between photon energy and frequency.

q: The above relation is known as ____ equation.
e: The equation E=hv is known as Planck's equation.

q: The most important consequence of photoelectric effect leads to the concept of wave-particle ____ nature of either particles or waves.
e: The photoelectric effect demonstrates that light exhibits both wave-like and particle-like properties.

q: That means light behaves sometimes as a particle and the other times behaves like a ____.
e: This duality is a fundamental concept in quantum mechanics.

q: Isotopes are the atoms of the same element with different ____.
e: Isotopes of an element have the same number of protons but different masses.

q: That is, they have the same number of protons but have different number of ____.
e: The difference in mass among isotopes is due to a varying number of neutrons in the nucleus.

q: In other words, isotopes have the same atomic number but have different ____ number.
e: The mass number is the sum of protons and neutrons, which varies among isotopes.

q: Since isotopes of an element have same number of electrons, they have same electron configuration and thereby have the same ____ properties.
e: Chemical properties are determined by electron configuration, which is identical for isotopes of the same element.

q: They have different ____ properties as they vary in their atomic mass.
e: Physical properties, such as density and boiling point, can differ slightly due to the mass difference.

q: Some isotopes are ____, that is, they do not decay (or transform) into other elements.
e: Stable isotopes have a balanced nucleus and do not undergo radioactive decay.

q: However, some are unstable (or ____), that is, decay into other elements.
e: Radioactive isotopes have unstable nuclei that spontaneously decay, emitting radiation.

q: Stable isotopes and some radioactive isotopes (____) exist naturally.
e: Radioisotopes are the naturally occurring or artificially produced radioactive forms of elements.

q: Isotopes can also be produced artificially using nuclear reactors and particle ____.
e: Artificial isotopes are created by bombarding stable nuclei with particles in accelerators or reactors.

q: Every chemical element has one or more ____.
e: All elements have at least one isotope, and many have several.

q: For example, copper has two stable isotopes: ____ and $^{65}\text{Cu}$.
e: Copper-63 and Copper-65 are the two naturally occurring stable isotopes of copper.

q: Three isotopes of hydrogen are: 1H (hydrogen), 2H(deuterium), and 3H(____).
e: Tritium is the heaviest and radioactive isotope of hydrogen.

q: Tritium is ____. It transforms into helium isotope 3He.
e: Tritium undergoes beta decay to become a stable isotope of helium.

q: Of over 1000 isotopes known thus far, the most abundant one in the entire universe is the hydrogen isotope ____.
e: Protium ($^1\text{H}$) is the simplest and most abundant isotope in the universe.

q: In studying cosmology, we get the information of celestial objects by the ____ they emit.
e: Astronomers analyze the light from celestial objects to determine their properties.

q: Their wavelengths are measured to obtain the astronomical ____.
e: Astronomical spectra provide crucial data about the composition, temperature, and motion of celestial objects.

q: When a source of light waves is travelling away from the observer, the observed wavelength will be slightly ____ than the wavelength of the stationary (rest) source.
e: The Doppler effect causes the wavelength to stretch when the source moves away.

q: In astronomy, this shift toward longer wavelengths is referred to as a ____ since red is at the long-wavelength end of the visible spectrum.
e: Redshift indicates that an astronomical object is moving away from the observer.

q: Conversely, a shift toward shorter wavelength, which occurs when the source is moving toward the observer, is called a ____.
e: Blueshift indicates that an astronomical object is approaching the observer.

q: The main reasons for redshift are as follows: ____ effect i.e., the movement of objects either closer or apart from each other in space.
e: The Doppler effect is a primary cause of redshift and blueshift due to relative motion.

q: Strong gravitational force leads to gravitational ____.
e: Light escaping a strong gravitational field loses energy, resulting in a gravitational redshift.

q: Cosmological redshift is such that light stretches (longer wavelength) as space ____.
e: The expansion of the universe itself stretches the wavelength of light traveling through it.

q: In 1929, ____ examined a series of velocity measurements for different galaxies.
e: Edwin Hubble's observations of galaxy velocities led to the formulation of Hubble's Law.

q: He noticed that the farther away the galaxy the faster it moved, and that the relationship was ____.
e: Hubble found a direct, linear proportionality between a galaxy's distance and its recession velocity.

q: This relationship between the velocity of a galaxy and its distance has come to be known as the ____ law.
e: Hubble's Law is a fundamental principle in physical cosmology.

q: It provided the first evidence that the Universe is ____, a result that was rather startling at that time, as it had long been assumed that the Universe was static and unchanging.
e: Hubble's Law revolutionized astronomy by proving the universe is not static but expanding.

q: Hubble's law formula is given as follows: v = ____.
e: The formula relates recession velocity (v) to distance (d) via the Hubble constant ($H_0$).

q: where v is the velocity of the galaxy in km s^-1, H0 is the Hubble ____ in km s^-1 (Mpc)^-1, d is the distance between the observer and the galaxy in Mpc.
e: The Hubble constant represents the rate of expansion of the universe.

q: Because of the intrinsic motion of galaxies, observed ____ gets influenced.
e: Local gravitational interactions can cause peculiar velocities that complicate Hubble's Law measurements.

q: Galaxy orbiting due to gravitational ____.
e: Gravitational movements within clusters can affect the observed recession velocity of individual galaxies.

q: Hubble constant is defined as the unit of measurement, which is used for describing the ____ of the universe.
e: The Hubble constant quantifies the current rate of the universe's expansion.

q: Hubble constant is ____ km s^-1 (Mpc)^-1.
e: The textbook uses an approximate value of 72 km s^-1 (Mpc)^-1 for the Hubble constant.

q: The redshift formula is given as, z = ____.
e: For non-relativistic speeds, redshift z is approximately equal to the recession velocity divided by the speed of light.

q: where z is the redshift, Δλ is the shift in wavelength in the spectra, λ is the wavelength, v is the ____ velocity of space object, c is the speed of light.
e: Recession velocity is the speed at which an object is moving away from the observer.

q: The Hubble time or age of the universe is defined as the ____ of the Hubble constant.
e: The Hubble time is a rough estimate of the age of the universe, calculated as $1/H_0$.

q: Hubble time is given as follows: tH = ____.
e: This formula provides the Hubble time, representing the time since the Big Bang if the expansion rate were constant.

q: t = ____ years.
e: The calculated Hubble time is approximately $1.36\times 10^{10}$ years.

q: t = ____ billion years.
e: This corresponds to an estimated age of the universe of 13.6 billion years.

q: The Hubble length is defined as the product of the speed of light and the Hubble ____.
e: The Hubble length represents the distance light could have traveled since the Big Bang in a linearly expanding universe.

q: It is also known as the Hubble ____.
e: Hubble length and Hubble distance are synonymous terms in cosmology.

q: The Hubble volume is defined as the volume of the ____ universe (visible universe).
e: The Hubble volume encompasses the region of the universe from which light has had time to reach us.

q: It is also defined as the volume of sphere whose radius is ____.
e: The radius of this spherical volume is the Hubble length, $c/H_0$.
